idiom_name: Sequel dataset CRUD returning hash rows (Sequel::Model kept for Active Record use cases)
implementation_notes: Ruby's database toolkit makes the per-row object largely unnecessary: Sequel::Dataset answers insert/update/delete for a filtered dataset and returns rows as symbol-keyed hashes, so the classic gateway collapses into dataset chains and the finder becomes .where(id: id).first. When a real object per row is wanted, Sequel::Model (and ActiveRecord::Base) provides one - but it is documented as the Active Record pattern and adds domain logic, so use it deliberately rather than as a stand-in for a gateway. Write an explicit gateway class only when you need object identity or a stable API in front of the dataset, and keep it free of domain rules.
code_sketch:
DB = Sequel.connect(ENV.fetch('DATABASE_URL'))

def find_person(id)   = DB[:people].where(id: id).first          # => Hash or nil
def insert_person(attrs) = DB[:people].insert(attrs)            # => new id
def update_person(id, attrs) = DB[:people].where(id: id).update(attrs)
def delete_person(id) = DB[:people].where(id: id).delete
pitfalls: Hash rows couple callers to column names, and a typo returns nil instead of raising unless you add a schema or model layer.
Sequel::Model instances are Active Record: adding behaviour there quietly changes the pattern, and its hooks/callbacks make the persistence path implicit.
A dataset method is per call, so a loop that fetches one row at a time is an N+1 waiting to happen; use a single dataset query.
Databases and models share a connection pool - holding a model reference across threads or requests is safe only as long as the pool, not the connection, is what you keep.
